Product Design.intro: Turn a user problem into a clear, testable interface.

modules.title: Notice a usability problem
modules.overview: Good design starts with a specific person and a real task, not a screen full of decoration.
modules.activity: Choose a small task you know well, such as finding a bus time or booking an appointment. Write down who is doing it, what they need, and where they might get stuck.
modules.deliverable: A one-page problem statement with a user, need, and three observations.
checklist: Describe one user and one task
Separate observations from assumptions
Name one question you still need to answer

modules.title: Sketch the simplest flow
modules.overview: A few rough screens can expose confusing steps before you spend time polishing them.
modules.activity: Draw the happy path for your task in four to six boxes. Label each action and show what the user sees next.
modules.deliverable: A photographed or digital flow sketch.
checklist: Start from a clear entry point
Give every screen one main action
Include a useful empty or error state

modules.title: Make a clickable prototype
modules.overview: Connect the core screens so another person can try the task without your help.
modules.activity: Build a low-fidelity prototype in a tool you can access, or link simple HTML screens. Ask one person to complete the task and observe silently.
modules.deliverable: A shareable prototype and three notes from a usability test.
checklist: The core task can be completed
The test participant knows what to do next
At least one observation leads to a change

modules.title: Improve and explain your design
modules.overview: A short case study makes your decisions and learning visible.
modules.activity: Update the prototype, then explain the problem, the first idea, what you observed, and what you changed.
modules.deliverable: A one-page case study with prototype link and next question.
checklist: Show the before and after
Connect each change to evidence
Credit any assets you did not create

Product Management.intro: Learn to turn a user problem into a focused product decision.

modules.title: Frame the user problem
modules.overview: A product brief starts with a person and a difficulty, not a feature request.
modules.activity: Pick a familiar service. Interview one willing person about a recent task and ask what was hard, what they tried, and what success looked like.
modules.deliverable: A problem statement and three interview notes with identifying details removed.
checklist: Describe a specific user and situation
Quote evidence rather than guess
Write one open question

modules.title: Choose a measurable outcome
modules.overview: A useful outcome describes a user change that can be observed.
modules.activity: Write one desired user outcome and a simple measure. Note one guardrail that would catch a harmful shortcut.
modules.deliverable: An outcome statement with a measure, baseline to collect, and guardrail.
checklist: Measure user success rather than output
Say how the measure would be collected
Name a possible unintended effect

modules.title: Prioritize a small experiment
modules.overview: Small tests reduce uncertainty before a team commits to a large build.
modules.activity: List three possible solutions. Compare user value, effort, and uncertainty. Choose the smallest ethical experiment that could change your mind.
modules.deliverable: A one-page experiment brief with hypothesis, steps, and decision rule.
checklist: State a falsifiable hypothesis
Include a stop or change decision
Avoid collecting unnecessary personal data

modules.title: Share a product recommendation
modules.overview: A concise recommendation makes trade-offs and evidence easy to review.
modules.activity: Summarize the problem, evidence, chosen experiment, risks, and what you would do next.
modules.deliverable: A short product memo or three-slide presentation.
checklist: Separate fact from assumption
Explain one trade-off
List what evidence could change your recommendation

AI & Machine Learning.intro: Build a small, responsible data project and explain its limits.

modules.title: Ask a question before choosing a model
modules.overview: A model is only useful when the task, data, and consequences are understood.
modules.activity: Choose a public, non-sensitive dataset. Write the question it could help answer and who might be affected by a wrong answer.
modules.deliverable: A project card with question, intended users, and risk notes.
checklist: Use data with a clear public licence
Do not use sensitive personal records
Describe what the model should not decide

modules.title: Inspect and prepare the data
modules.overview: Simple checks often reveal missing values, skew, leakage, and uneven representation.
modules.activity: Use a spreadsheet or notebook to inspect column meanings, missing values, class balance, and a simple baseline. Keep a note of each transformation.
modules.deliverable: A data dictionary and a short data-quality note.
checklist: Identify the source and licence
Check missingness and class balance
Keep target information out of input features

modules.title: Compare a baseline fairly
modules.overview: A transparent baseline is a useful benchmark, not proof that a system is ready for use.
modules.activity: Split data before tuning. Compare a simple baseline with one small model using a metric suited to the question. Record the split and limitations.
modules.deliverable: A reproducible notebook or script with results and limitations.
checklist: Keep a held-out test set
Choose a metric for the task
Do not claim results generalize beyond the data

modules.title: Write a model card
modules.overview: A model card communicates intended use, evaluation, and where the model can fail.
modules.activity: Write who the experiment is for, how you tested it, where results were weak, and what review would be needed before deployment.
modules.deliverable: A one-page model card linked to your notebook.
checklist: State intended and out-of-scope uses
Report failure cases and uncertainty
Do not present a demo as a production system

Data & Analytics.intro: Turn a clear question into a trustworthy, understandable insight.

modules.title: Define the decision and the metric
modules.overview: Analysis is most useful when it helps someone make a specific decision.
modules.activity: Pick a public dataset and write the decision a reader might make. Define one primary metric and what counts in its numerator and denominator.
modules.deliverable: A question-and-metric brief.
checklist: Name the intended decision
Define the metric precisely
Identify what the metric does not capture

modules.title: Clean and validate a dataset
modules.overview: Documented cleaning makes an analysis easier to reproduce and challenge.
modules.activity: Inspect types, duplicates, missing values, date ranges, and unusual values in a spreadsheet or notebook. Record changes rather than silently dropping rows.
modules.deliverable: A cleaned dataset or reproducible cleaning steps with a change log.
checklist: Record the source and licence
Quantify rows changed or removed
Check totals before and after cleaning

modules.title: Build a decision-focused report
modules.overview: A good chart answers one question and makes its scale and caveats clear.
modules.activity: Create two useful charts and a short summary. Include the period, units, sample size, and one limitation.
modules.deliverable: A compact dashboard, notebook, or two-page analysis.
checklist: Label axes and units
Use a scale that does not mislead
Connect each chart to a decision

modules.title: Present a recommendation with caveats
modules.overview: Insights become actionable when the recommendation is proportionate to the evidence.
modules.activity: Present the question, method, result, recommendation, and what additional data would change your conclusion.
modules.deliverable: A five-minute presentation or written executive summary.
checklist: Distinguish correlation from causation
Explain uncertainty and missing data
Protect private or identifying information

Cybersecurity.intro: Practice defensive security on systems and data you own or are authorized to test.

modules.title: Map a safe practice environment
modules.overview: Security skills begin with clear authorization and an understanding of what needs protection.
modules.activity: Use a local demo app or a deliberately vulnerable training lab. Draw its components and list the data or accounts that matter. Do not scan public systems.
modules.deliverable: A small system diagram and authorization/scope note.
checklist: Use only a lab you control or have permission to test
Identify valuable data and trust boundaries
Write down what is out of scope

modules.title: Review basic account and web defenses
modules.overview: A careful configuration review helps prevent common, avoidable security mistakes.
modules.activity: For your local lab, review password handling, session cookie flags, input validation, and dependency versions. Record observations without attempting to access real accounts.
modules.deliverable: A defensive checklist with evidence and prioritized recommendations.
checklist: Do not test against third-party targets
Support each observation with local evidence
Prioritize fixes by impact and likelihood

modules.title: Harden the demo app
modules.overview: A useful security project shows a safe fix and a regression check, not just a list of issues.
modules.activity: Choose one issue in the lab, make a minimal defensive change, and add a test showing the expected safe behavior.
modules.deliverable: A patch or configuration diff, test, and short rationale.
checklist: Make changes only in the authorized lab
Avoid publishing secrets or personal data
Verify the fix with a repeatable test

modules.title: Write a responsible security report
modules.overview: A clear report explains impact and remediation while minimizing exposure.
modules.activity: Document scope, safe reproduction conditions in the lab, impact, fix, and verification. Remove secrets and identifying user data.
modules.deliverable: A concise defensive report for a maintainer.
checklist: State authorization and scope
Give remediation steps
Do not include real credentials or exploit unrelated systems

Digital Marketing.intro: Practice an accessible, measurable campaign with honest claims.

modules.title: Understand the audience and goal
modules.overview: A campaign should solve a real audience need and have one clear objective.
modules.activity: Choose a product or community you know. Describe the audience using non-sensitive traits and write one goal for a small campaign.
modules.deliverable: A campaign brief with audience, need, and goal.
checklist: Avoid stereotypes and sensitive targeting
Make the goal measurable
State the audience need in plain language

modules.title: Write a clear message
modules.overview: Specific, truthful messaging helps people decide whether an offer is right for them.
modules.activity: Draft a headline, short description, and call to action. Check each factual claim and create alt text for one visual.
modules.deliverable: A small copy and creative brief.
checklist: Substantiate factual claims
Use accessible and inclusive language
Do not use deceptive urgency

modules.title: Plan a small experiment
modules.overview: A controlled, privacy-conscious test can improve a campaign without over-collecting data.
modules.activity: Choose one variable to test, define a success measure and a time window, and state what personal data you will avoid collecting.
modules.deliverable: A one-page experiment plan with sample messages.
checklist: Change one main variable at a time
Define a stop rule and success threshold
Use consent and data minimization

modules.title: Review results responsibly
modules.overview: A result is more useful when its sample size and limitations are visible.
modules.activity: Use clearly labelled example or consented data to summarize results. Explain uncertainty and one next experiment.
modules.deliverable: A short campaign report with a chart and recommendation.
checklist: Label simulated data as simulated
Include sample size and dates
Do not infer more than the data supports

Software Engineering.intro: Build a small, tested feature and make it easy for someone else to run.

modules.title: Turn a need into a small specification
modules.overview: A narrow, testable requirement keeps a first project achievable.
modules.activity: Pick a small everyday problem. Write one user story, two acceptance criteria, and one case the feature should reject or handle safely.
modules.deliverable: A short feature specification.
checklist: Describe one user need
Make acceptance criteria observable
Include a failure or edge case

modules.title: Build the smallest working version
modules.overview: A simple vertical slice is easier to understand than a large unfinished feature.
modules.activity: Use a language and tools available to you. Build one working path from input to visible result and split the work into small commits if using Git.
modules.deliverable: A runnable first version in a repository you control.
checklist: Include clear setup instructions
Handle invalid input
Do not commit passwords, tokens, or private data

modules.title: Add tests and a useful interface
modules.overview: Tests make expected behavior repeatable, and clear interface states help users recover.
modules.activity: Add tests for the main path and one failure case. Make loading, empty, success, and error states understandable.
modules.deliverable: A working feature, tests, and screenshots or a short demo.
checklist: Test the acceptance criteria
Test one invalid or unavailable case
Keep controls keyboard and mobile friendly

modules.title: Prepare a maintainable handoff
modules.overview: A project is stronger when another person can run it and understand your decisions.
modules.activity: Write the setup, tests, design choices, known limitations, and the next small improvement.
modules.deliverable: A project README and short retrospective.
checklist: Verify instructions from a clean setup
Credit and licence third-party assets
List limitations honestly

Not sure yet.intro: Try a short discovery sprint and use your observations to choose a direction.

modules.title: Map what gives you energy
modules.overview: Career discovery is about finding patterns in tasks you enjoy and skills you want to practice.
modules.activity: List three activities you enjoy, three things people ask you for help with, and one kind of problem you want to understand better.
modules.deliverable: A personal strengths and curiosity map.
checklist: Focus on activities, not job titles
Include what you want to learn
Treat this as a draft, not a permanent choice

modules.title: Try three mini career tasks
modules.overview: A small sample of real work can tell you more than a job-title description.
modules.activity: Spend 20 minutes each sketching a screen, writing a simple data question, and outlining a small program or campaign. Note which felt most engaging.
modules.deliverable: Three rough samples and a short reflection.
checklist: Keep each task low-pressure
Note what felt interesting or frustrating
Do not compare beginner samples to expert work

modules.title: Choose one tiny project
modules.overview: A small finished project is a practical way to explore one path without a large commitment.
modules.activity: Choose the mini task you enjoyed most. Make one small artifact, show it to someone you trust, and ask what is clear or confusing.
modules.deliverable: One artifact with feedback notes.
checklist: Choose a project you can finish
Ask for specific, kind feedback
Make one change based on what you learned

modules.title: Choose your next experiment
modules.overview: A career direction can be an experiment that you revisit as you learn.
modules.activity: Write down one path you want to explore next, why it interests you, and one free resource or person you can learn from.
modules.deliverable: A two-week learning goal.
checklist: Choose a goal that fits your available time
Use a resource you can access for free
Set a date to reflect and adjust
